screens.title: Data Ingestion and ETL with Azure SQL
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to move data into Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance with reliability and performance. We start by contrasting simple T-S Q L inserts with high-performance bulk loading methods, and then show how orchestration tools like Azure Data Factory and SSIS help you automate transformations and error handling. You will see concrete examples for BULK INSERT flows, a Copy Data activity in Azure Data Factory, and a practical hands-on simulation for loading product data. Along the way we'll emphasize critical operational practices: staging raw data before transformation, batching large loads, temporarily dropping nonclustered indexes during bulk loads, and securely managing credentials for external storage. These practices protect production tables, speed ingestion, and make recovery deterministic. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right ingestion method for a scenario, outline an ADF pipeline for incremental loads, and apply staging and error-handling patterns so large loads are both fast and safe. Consider how you would approach a daily incremental feed to Azure S Q L—what staging and error paths would you add?

These skills reduce downtime, improve throughput, and make ingestion repeatable. Think about a dataset you maintain: which objective would most reduce your daily load time?

screens.title: What is data ingestion for Azure SQL?
screens.narratorSegment: Data ingestion means moving data from source systems into a target database so it can be processed, analyzed, or reported on. For Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance, ingestion covers small ad-hoc inserts as well as multi-terabyte bulk transfers. Practically, ingestion is more than copying bytes. It includes preparing the data, ensuring secure access, validating schema, and choosing a method that balances speed and safety. For example, inserting a few hundred rows from a form can use simple T-S Q L INSERT statements. By contrast, loading millions of historical rows requires bulk mechanisms and a staging area to validate content before merging with production. A common misconception is that faster always means unsafe; without staging and error handling, a fast bulk load can overwrite or corrupt production data if invalid rows slip through. Another misunderstanding is assuming the same approach fits both cloud-native Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance; Managed Instance may support network shares, while Azure S Q L Database expects blob storage access via configured external data sources. Key takeaway: treat ingestion as a process that must be designed — not just a single command. Ask yourself which properties matter most for each load: data volume, schema stability, transformation complexity, and recovery requirements.

keyIdea.title: Ingestion as a designed process
keyIdea.text: Choose methods based on volume, transformation needs, and security, and always include staging and validation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is data ingestion?
Definition
Moving data from sources into Azure SQL for processing, reporting, and analytics while ensuring correctness and security.
Why it matters
  • Ensures reliable downstream reporting and analytics
  • Prevents production outages from failed loads
  • Makes recovery and auditing possible with staging and logs
Common misconceptions
Faster equals better — without validation, speed can compromise data quality. One-size-fits-all — different targets and volumes need different approaches.
Concrete example
Imagine migrating three years of transactional history from an on-premises database to an Azure SQL Managed Instance. You would export to files, bulk load into staging tables, validate dates and keys, then merge into fact tables with transactional control. This prevents corrupt rows from entering production and allows selective retries.
Key takeaway
Design ingestion with staging, validation, and secured access to external files.
Pitfall
Loading directly into production without staging risks partial failures and corruption.

screens.title: T-SQL INSERTs vs Bulk loading
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between direct T-S Q L INSERTs and bulk loading methods starts with volume and frequency. Use straightforward INSERT INTO... VALUES or INSERT INTO... SELECT for small ad-hoc loads and transactional inserts, where each row matters and latency is low. However, when you move large datasets — thousands to millions of rows — you should shift to bulk loading with BULK INSERT or the bcp utility. Bulk methods read files in an optimized path and can dramatically reduce input and output and logging overhead. A useful mental model: if the load will take a few seconds, T-S Q L inserts are fine; if it will take minutes or more, plan for bulk techniques plus staging. Another nuance is transform complexity. If significant transformations are required during ingestion, consider whether to transform in an intermediate processing layer, or use ADF or SSIS to perform transformation before or after bulk load. A misconception is thinking bcp and BULK INSERT are identical in all environments. Functionally they both perform bulk copy, but bcp is a command-line tool useful in scripting and automation, while BULK INSERT is a T-S Q L statement that runs inside the server context and requires proper external data source configuration for Azure S Q L. Before choosing, ask: how large is the dataset, does the target allow direct file access, and will I need to validate rows before merging?

keyIdea.text: Small transactional loads use T-SQL. Large, high-throughput loads require BULK INSERT or bcp with staging and validation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › T-SQL vs Bulk
T-SQL INSERT
Best for small, transactional inserts and quick ad-hoc tasks. Easy to write and debug but can be slow for very large row counts due to logging and row-by-row operations.
Pros
  • Simple and transactional
  • Runs inside database context
Cons
  • Poor throughput on large datasets
Bulk loading (BULK INSERT / bcp)
Designed for high-volume imports. Use staging tables and batch sizes, and ensure external data source and credentials for Azure Blob access when required.
Pros
  • High performance and lower logging overhead
  • Suitable for scripted automation
Cons
  • Requires external data source configuration and staging
Checklist before choosing
Data volume estimate
Transform complexity
Access to files/storage

screens.title: BULK INSERT example and workflow
screens.narratorSegment: BULK INSERT is a T-S Q L statement that imports a file directly into a table. It’s fast because it uses a streamlined data path into the engine. In Azure, the file often resides in Blob Storage and you must configure an external data source and possibly a database-scoped credential so the database can access the file securely. The typical workflow is: create a staging table that mirrors the incoming file, run BULK INSERT into staging with options for format, terminators, and first row, validate and clean the staging rows, and then MERGE into production tables inside a transaction. The MERGE step allows updates for existing keys and inserts for new keys; it’s a safe place to map staging columns to production columns. A common misconception is to skip staging and bulk directly into the production table — this risks partial failures and complex rollbacks. Here is a concrete server-side example you can run in Azure Data Studio after configuring storage access. Use staging to verify types and check for unexpected nulls before merging. After successful merge, drop or truncate staging as part of your pipeline’s cleanup step. How would you validate dates and foreign-key mappings in the staging area before merging?

keyIdea.title: BULK INSERT pattern
keyIdea.text: Use an external data source + staging table, validate rows, then MERGE into production with transactional control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › BULK INSERT walkthrough
Workflow steps
  1. Create staging table representing raw file fields
  2. Configure external data source and credentials for blob access
  3. Run BULK INSERT with format and batch options
  4. Validate and transform rows in staging
  5. MERGE into production within a controlled transaction
Key tip
Use FIRSTROW to skip headers and enable batch sizes to limit transaction log growth during imports.
Example — BULK INSERT + MERGE
-- Assume 'mydataengdb' is the target database
USE mydataengdb;
GO

-- Create a temporary staging table for bulk import
CREATE TABLE StagingOrders (
    OrderID INT,
    CustomerID INT,
    OrderDate DATE,
    TotalAmount DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
GO

BULK INSERT StagingOrders
FROM 'https://yourstorageaccount.blob.core.windows.net/data/orders.csv'
WITH (
    DATA_SOURCE = 'MyAzureBlobStorage',
    FORMAT = 'CSV',
    FIELDTERMINATOR = ',',
    ROWTERMINATOR = '
',
    FIRSTROW = 2
);
GO

-- After bulk insert, transform and merge
MERGE INTO FactSales AS Target
USING StagingOrders AS Source
ON Target.OrderID = Source.OrderID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET
        Target.OrderDate = Source.OrderDate,
        Target.TotalAmount = Source.TotalAmount
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (DateKey, ProductKey, CustomerKey, Quantity, UnitPrice)
    VALUES (
        (SELECT DateKey FROM DimDate WHERE FullDate = Source.OrderDate),
        (SELECT ProductKey FROM DimProduct WHERE ProductID = Source.ProductID),
        Source.CustomerID,
        Source.Quantity,
        Source.UnitPrice
    );
GO

screens.title: bcp utility and automation
screens.narratorSegment: The bcp utility is a command-line tool that exports and imports data between a S Q L Server instance and a data file. It’s useful for scripted automation and scenarios where you run data movement from a client or integration server rather than inside the database. In automation pipelines, bcp is commonly invoked in shell scripts or scheduled jobs to create flat files for archival or to push files into a staging landing zone. A common use case is moving data from an on-premises server to an intermediary file share that can then be uploaded to Blob Storage for consumption by Azure S Q L. A key advantage is that bcp runs outside the database process, so it can be orchestrated with other tasks like compression and secure transfer. A typical misconception is thinking bcp eliminates the need for staging or validation — it does not. Whether you use bcp or BULK INSERT, you still should land into staging tables and perform validation before merging into production. When scripting bcp, also consider network reliability and logging so failed transfers can be retried or inspected. Finally, bcp complements ADF and SSIS by providing a lightweight, scriptable option for legacy automation and migrations.

keyIdea.text: Use bcp when you need a client-side, scriptable bulk copy tool as part of an automation pipeline; still use staging and validation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › bcp & automation
Where bcp fits
Client-side bulk copy for scripted, scheduled, or legacy workflows. Useful for producing files or ingesting from files when server-side access is limited.
Scenarios
  • Exporting snapshots to files for transfer
  • Importing prepared files into staging via automation
  • Complementing tools like ADF and SSIS in migration paths
Best practices
  • Log and checkpoint transfers for retries
  • Validate schema and sample rows after import
  • Combine with secure copy to blob storage for Azure consumption
Pro tip
Use bcp in a script that produces compressed files and then upload to Blob Storage for ADF or BULK INSERT to consume.

screens.title: Azure Data Factory: Copy Data activity
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Data Factory is the orchestration layer you reach for when ingestion needs scheduling, monitoring, and robust error handling. The core building block is the Copy Data activity that moves data between a source and a sink. In ADF you declare datasets and linked services, then construct a pipeline that may include a pre-copy script — for example, truncating a staging table — and settings that redirect incompatible rows to a storage path for later inspection. Incremental loads are implemented by selecting changed rows only or by maintaining watermarks in control tables. The Copy Data activity can write into Azure S Q L with different write behaviors such as Insert, Upsert, or DeleteAndInsert. Resilience comes from enabling skip or redirect for incompatible rows and from instrumented retries and alerts. A common mistake is not capturing incompatible rows; without redirection you silently lose data or fail the entire pipeline. The snippet shown in the lesson is a simplified JSON representation of a Copy activity that includes a preCopyScript and redirect settings. When designing pipelines, also plan monitoring: track top failing rows, latency, and compute usage. How will you capture and replay incompatible rows in your pipeline?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › ADF Copy Activity
Design patterns
  • Use pre-copy scripts to prepare staging tables
  • Enable redirect of incompatible rows for inspection
  • Implement incremental loads with watermarks
  • Instrument with monitoring and retries
Example — Copy activity JSON (simplified)
{
    "name": "CopyDataToAzureSQL",
    "type": "Copy",
    "inputs": [
        { "referenceName": "SourceBlobDataset", "type": "DatasetReference" }
    ],
    "outputs": [
        { "referenceName": "TargetAzureSQLDataset", "type": "DatasetReference" }
    ],
    "typeProperties": {
        "source": {
            "type": "DelimitedTextSource",
            "storeSettings": {
                "type": "AzureBlobStorageReadSettings",
                "recursive": true
            }
        },
        "sink": {
            "type": "SqlDBSink",
            "writeBehavior": "Insert",
            "sqlWriterUseTableLock": true,
            "preCopyScript": "TRUNCATE TABLE [dbo].[StagingTable];"
        },
        "enableSkipIncompatibleRow": true,
        "redirectIncompatibleRowSettings": {
            "linkedServiceName": { "referenceName": "AzureBlobStorageLinkedService", "type": "LinkedServiceReference" },
            "path": "errorlogs/"
        }
    }
}

screens.title: SSIS Integration Runtime and hybrid scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: Organizations with a history of SSIS packages can move those investments to Azure by using SSIS Integration Runtime within Azure Data Factory. This allows running existing packages in a managed Azure environment, preserving complex transformation logic and connections to on-premises systems. SSIS IR is particularly valuable in hybrid scenarios where sources remain on-premises or where packages contain business rules that are costly to rewrite. The migration pattern is: deploy SSIS projects to an SSIS catalog hosted in Azure S Q L or Managed Instance, configure the Integration Runtime, and execute packages as pipeline activities in ADF. A common misconception is that migration requires rewriting all logic; in many cases, you can lift-and-shift the package and then incrementally modernize. That said, evaluate operational dependencies—packages that rely on local files or drivers may need rework. Use SSIS IR when the cost and risk of rewriting outweigh refactoring. Also plan monitoring, credential management, and redeployment strategies. A reflective question: which of your SSIS packages are good candidates for lift-and-shift, and which would benefit from redesign into Data Flow or Databricks work? SSIS Integration Runtime and hybrid scenarios means use ssis integration runtime to run existing packages in azure when hybrid connectivity or complex transforms make rewriting expensive.. In practical terms, when to lift-and-shift ssis packages to azure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › SSIS Integration Runtime
Lift-and-shift pattern
Deploy existing SSIS projects to an SSIS catalog in Azure SQL or Managed Instance and execute them using an SSIS Integration Runtime in ADF.
Benefits

screens.title: Best practices for reliable and efficient ingestion
screens.narratorSegment: Efficient and fault-tolerant ingestion depends on several operational practices. First, always land raw data into staging tables. This isolates incoming errors and lets you apply validation rules before touching production schemas. Second, use batching to limit transaction sizes and control log growth during bulk loads. Third, manage nonclustered indexes: drop or disable them before a large bulk load and rebuild after to speed ingestion, remembering that rebuilding consumes resources. Fourth, implement robust error handling: redirect incompatible rows in ADF or log errors during BULK INSERT so problematic rows can be replayed. Fifth, use transactions to group multi-step loads so either all steps succeed or all are rolled back, maintaining atomicity. Sixth, secure credentials: store connection strings and secrets in Azure Key Vault and use database-scoped credentials or managed identities for storage access. A common pitfall is adding indexes preemptively without checking their write penalty, which can slow ingestion. Another is neglecting monitoring; without observing load durations and failure rates, you cannot improve. Key takeaway: pair a fast load mechanism with staging and visibility so you can recover and iterate safely. Which of these practices is easiest for you to adopt immediately?

Staging tables for raw data and validation

screens.title: Simulated BULK INSERT in Azure Data Studio
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on simulation shows how to practice bulk ingestion when a direct BULK INSERT from a local file isn't available for Azure S Q L Database. keyIdea.title: Simulate safely
keyIdea.text: Use multi-row INSERTs in Azure Data Studio to practice staging, validation, and merge before performing a true BULK INSERT in production.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Hands-on: Simulated BULK INSERT
Steps to simulate a bulk load
  1. Ensure the database and target table exist
  2. Create or truncate a staging table
  3. Insert multiple rows in a single statement to simulate a file load
  4. Validate staging rows with queries
  5. MERGE into production tables inside a transaction
Safety note
For Azure SQL Database, real BULK INSERT requires blob storage access. This simulation teaches process and validation without external file setup.
Example SQL (simulated bulk insert)
USE mydataengdb;
GO

-- Drop and re-create DimProduct for a clean start
IF OBJECT_ID('DimProduct', 'U') IS NOT NULL DROP TABLE DimProduct;
GO

CREATE TABLE DimProduct (
    ProductKey INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    ProductID NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    ProductName NVARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    Category NVARCHAR(100)
);
GO

-- Simulate bulk insert by inserting multiple rows at once
INSERT INTO DimProduct (ProductID, ProductName, Category) VALUES
('P001', 'Laptop X1', 'Electronics'),
('P002', 'Monitor Ultra', 'Electronics'),
('P003', 'Webcam HD', 'Accessories'),
('P004', 'Gaming Keyboard', 'Accessories');
GO

-- Verify the inserted data
SELECT * FROM DimProduct;

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to move data into Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance with reliability and performance. We start by contrasting simple T-S Q L inserts with high-performance bulk loading methods, and then show how orchestration tools like Azure Data Factory and SSIS help you automate transformations and error handling. You will see concrete examples for BULK INSERT flows, a Copy Data activity in Azure Data Factory, and a practical hands-on simulation for loading product data. Along the way we'll emphasize critical operational practices: staging raw data before transformation, batching large loads, temporarily dropping nonclustered indexes during bulk loads, and securely managing credentials for external storage. These practices protect production tables, speed ingestion, and make recovery deterministic. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose the right ingestion method for a scenario, outline an ADF pipeline for incremental loads, and apply staging and error-handling patterns so large loads are both fast and safe. Consider how you would approach a daily incremental feed to Azure S Q L—what staging and error paths would you add?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose and configure ingestion methods for Azure S Q L, implement high-performance bulk loads, and design pipelines that preserve data quality. First, you will learn to identify which tool fits a scenario — from simple T-S Q L inserts for small sets to BULK INSERT and bcp for large files. Second, you'll implement bulk loading techniques including staging patterns, batch sizing, and index handling so loads finish faster and safely. Third, you'll use Azure Data Factory to build Copy Data activities and data flows for orchestrated ETL, including pre-copy scripts and error redirection. Finally, you'll understand how SSIS Integration Runtime fits hybrid landscapes and when to lift-and-shift existing packages. Each objective includes a concrete outcome, such as creating a Copy Data pipeline that performs an incremental load with error redirection or running a BULK INSERT into a staging table and merging safely into a fact table. These skills reduce downtime, improve throughput, and make ingestion repeatable. Think about a dataset you maintain: which objective would most reduce your daily load time?

This page breaks objectives into actionable skills you can apply immediately. You will practice configuring an external data source or credential before attempting BULK INSERT from Azure Blob Storage, so you understand secure access patterns. You will create an ADF Copy Data activity with a pre-copy script to truncate staging and with error redirection to store incompatible rows. You will review an SSIS package migration strategy and decide when to use SSIS Integration Runtime to preserve complex transforms. Finally, you will implement batching and index management: either staging and merging or dropping and rebuilding nonclustered indexes to accelerate large loads. Each item has a milestone that verifies competency: successful BULK INSERT into staging and a verified merge into a fact table, a functioning ADF pipeline handling incompatible rows, and a documented SSIS lift-and-shift plan. Practically, these tasks reduce downtime and make rollbacks possible if something goes wrong. Which applied skill would you prioritize for your production pipeline this week?

Data ingestion means moving data from source systems into a target database so it can be processed, analyzed, or reported on. For Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance, ingestion covers small ad-hoc inserts as well as multi-terabyte bulk transfers. Practically, ingestion is more than copying bytes. It includes preparing the data, ensuring secure access, validating schema, and choosing a method that balances speed and safety. For example, inserting a few hundred rows from a form can use simple T-S Q L INSERT statements. By contrast, loading millions of historical rows requires bulk mechanisms and a staging area to validate content before merging with production. A common misconception is that faster always means unsafe; without staging and error handling, a fast bulk load can overwrite or corrupt production data if invalid rows slip through. Another misunderstanding is assuming the same approach fits both cloud-native Azure S Q L Database and Managed Instance; Managed Instance may support network shares, while Azure S Q L Database expects blob storage access via configured external data sources. Key takeaway: treat ingestion as a process that must be designed — not just a single command. Ask yourself which properties matter most for each load: data volume, schema stability, transformation complexity, and recovery requirements.

Choosing between direct T-S Q L INSERTs and bulk loading methods starts with volume and frequency. Use straightforward INSERT INTO... VALUES or INSERT INTO... SELECT for small ad-hoc loads and transactional inserts, where each row matters and latency is low. However, when you move large datasets — thousands to millions of rows — you should shift to bulk loading with BULK INSERT or the bcp utility. Bulk methods read files in an optimized path and can dramatically reduce input and output and logging overhead. A useful mental model: if the load will take a few seconds, T-S Q L inserts are fine; if it will take minutes or more, plan for bulk techniques plus staging. Another nuance is transform complexity. If significant transformations are required during ingestion, consider whether to transform in an intermediate processing layer, or use ADF or SSIS to perform transformation before or after bulk load. A misconception is thinking bcp and BULK INSERT are identical in all environments. Functionally they both perform bulk copy, but bcp is a command-line tool useful in scripting and automation, while BULK INSERT is a T-S Q L statement that runs inside the server context and requires proper external data source configuration for Azure S Q L. Before choosing, ask: how large is the dataset, does the target allow direct file access, and will I need to validate rows before merging?

BULK INSERT is a T-S Q L statement that imports a file directly into a table. It’s fast because it uses a streamlined data path into the engine. In Azure, the file often resides in Blob Storage and you must configure an external data source and possibly a database-scoped credential so the database can access the file securely. The typical workflow is: create a staging table that mirrors the incoming file, run BULK INSERT into staging with options for format, terminators, and first row, validate and clean the staging rows, and then MERGE into production tables inside a transaction. The MERGE step allows updates for existing keys and inserts for new keys; it’s a safe place to map staging columns to production columns. A common misconception is to skip staging and bulk directly into the production table — this risks partial failures and complex rollbacks. Here is a concrete server-side example you can run in Azure Data Studio after configuring storage access. Use staging to verify types and check for unexpected nulls before merging. After successful merge, drop or truncate staging as part of your pipeline’s cleanup step. How would you validate dates and foreign-key mappings in the staging area before merging?

The bcp utility is a command-line tool that exports and imports data between a S Q L Server instance and a data file. It’s useful for scripted automation and scenarios where you run data movement from a client or integration server rather than inside the database. In automation pipelines, bcp is commonly invoked in shell scripts or scheduled jobs to create flat files for archival or to push files into a staging landing zone. A common use case is moving data from an on-premises server to an intermediary file share that can then be uploaded to Blob Storage for consumption by Azure S Q L. A key advantage is that bcp runs outside the database process, so it can be orchestrated with other tasks like compression and secure transfer. A typical misconception is thinking bcp eliminates the need for staging or validation — it does not. Whether you use bcp or BULK INSERT, you still should land into staging tables and perform validation before merging into production. When scripting bcp, also consider network reliability and logging so failed transfers can be retried or inspected. Finally, bcp complements ADF and SSIS by providing a lightweight, scriptable option for legacy automation and migrations.

Azure Data Factory is the orchestration layer you reach for when ingestion needs scheduling, monitoring, and robust error handling. The core building block is the Copy Data activity that moves data between a source and a sink. In ADF you declare datasets and linked services, then construct a pipeline that may include a pre-copy script — for example, truncating a staging table — and settings that redirect incompatible rows to a storage path for later inspection. Incremental loads are implemented by selecting changed rows only or by maintaining watermarks in control tables. The Copy Data activity can write into Azure S Q L with different write behaviors such as Insert, Upsert, or DeleteAndInsert. Resilience comes from enabling skip or redirect for incompatible rows and from instrumented retries and alerts. A common mistake is not capturing incompatible rows; without redirection you silently lose data or fail the entire pipeline. The snippet shown in the lesson is a simplified JSON representation of a Copy activity that includes a preCopyScript and redirect settings. When designing pipelines, also plan monitoring: track top failing rows, latency, and compute usage. How will you capture and replay incompatible rows in your pipeline?

Organizations with a history of SSIS packages can move those investments to Azure by using SSIS Integration Runtime within Azure Data Factory. This allows running existing packages in a managed Azure environment, preserving complex transformation logic and connections to on-premises systems. SSIS IR is particularly valuable in hybrid scenarios where sources remain on-premises or where packages contain business rules that are costly to rewrite. The migration pattern is: deploy SSIS projects to an SSIS catalog hosted in Azure S Q L or Managed Instance, configure the Integration Runtime, and execute packages as pipeline activities in ADF. A common misconception is that migration requires rewriting all logic; in many cases, you can lift-and-shift the package and then incrementally modernize. That said, evaluate operational dependencies—packages that rely on local files or drivers may need rework. Use SSIS IR when the cost and risk of rewriting outweigh refactoring. Also plan monitoring, credential management, and redeployment strategies. A reflective question: which of your SSIS packages are good candidates for lift-and-shift, and which would benefit from redesign into Data Flow or Databricks work? SSIS Integration Runtime and hybrid scenarios means use ssis integration runtime to run existing packages in azure when hybrid connectivity or complex transforms make rewriting expensive.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
